newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Rice ship docks in besieged Freetown.
newsitem.headline: Rice ship docks in besieged Freetown.

text.p: A ship carrying 6,800 tonnes of rice beat a Nigerian blockade and received a rapturous welcome when it docked on Thursday in Freetown, capital of Sierra Leone, harbour authorities said.
"This is the first cargo boat to dock in Sierra Leone since the coup on May 25," a harbour official said, adding that a huge cheer had gone up when crowds on the waterfront saw the vessel.
Sierra Leone's West African neighbours have imposed an economic blockade on the country in an attempt to force the military junta to hand back power to ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
Diplomatic talks broke down on Wednesday and foreign ministers of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) said they would tighten the blockade as a result.
However, the Russia-flag Ivanov was able to dock with its cargo of rice under the escort of a Sierra Leone navy boat.
Junta spokesman Allieu Kamara said the government had instructed the harbour authorities to get the rice to market rapidly.

"The shipment of rice will last the country for about two to three months. We are also expecting a shipment of fuel, especially petrol and kerosene, to arrive in Freetown by ship over the weekend," Kamara added.
The Nigerian-led ECOWAS intervention force (ECOMOG) has been blockading the airport and land borders as well as the port, preventing food from arriving and sending prices soaring.
Residents say the cost of a bag of rice in Freetown has almost doubled to 40,000 leones ($50) from 22,000 on the eve of the coup. It is even higher in provincial towns, they added.
State radio warned traders earlier this month not to charge more than 25,000 a bag.
Economic sanctions are biting hard in Freetown.
Fuel for generators and transport is running out, leading to regular power cuts. Most people have no transport.
Most of the major banks have remained closed since the coup, preventing customers from getting at their savings.

Junta leader Johnny Paul Koroma said in a statement broadcast on Wednesday evening that the local branches of Barclays, Standard Chartered and other banks must open their doors by Monday or face liquidation.
Barclays and Standard Chartered are estimated to have about 80 percent of the banking market in Sierra Leone. The warning was also addressed to the Sierra Leone-owned Union Trust Bank.
The banks have said they would reopen when security improved.
State-owned Commercial Bank was obliged by the military to open for business on July 2.
Koroma called on foreign investors to help set up new banks to service agriculture, housing and industry.

The state would put up 45 percent of the capital and Sierra Leoneans 10 percent. "Foreign institutional investors will be invited to take 30 percent of the shares, while 15 percent will be offered to foreign private investors," he said.
